projects.title: Olevius
projects.blurb: Cuffless, wrist-worn blood pressure monitoring prototype using a custom fiber-optic sensor embedded in a PDMS pouch.

sections.title: Overview
body: Fourth-year Nanotechnology Engineering capstone project focused on continuous, non-invasive blood pressure monitoring at the wrist.
bullets: Developed as a proof-of-concept alternative to cuff-based monitoring and indirect optical wearable approaches.
Used a custom fiber-optic sensing element embedded in a glycerol-filled PDMS pouch to capture arterial pulse waveforms without a traditional cuff.
Integrated into a wrist-worn prototype with wireless signal streaming and mobile-app visualization.

sections.title: Problem
body: Continuous blood pressure monitoring is important for early detection of cardiovascular disease, but current methods are either invasive or uncomfortable for long-term use.

sections.title: My Role
body: I was the optomechanical lead, responsible for the core sensing hardware and physical integration of the device.
bullets: Built Python and COMSOL simulations.
Developed the fabrication and assembly processes for PDMS components and the fiber sensor.
Designed the wrist-mounted housing.

sections.title: Simulation & Design
bullets: Simulated mechanical deformation of the PDMS membrane and fluid-filled pouch under applied pressure using COMSOL.
Modeled how membrane deformation changed optical transmission across the fiber sensor gap.
Ran ray-based and diffraction-based simulations to estimate optical signal strength and inform hardware sensitivity requirements.
Used simulation results to optimize fiber gap length, predict signal levels, and reduce uncertainty before building the physical prototype.

sections.title: Sensor Fabrication
bullets: Designed and CNC-machined custom aluminum molds for the multilayer PDMS fluidic pouch.
Developed and optimized the fabrication and assembly process, including PDMS casting, bonding, and glycerol filling.
Produced dozens of sensor variants in order to optimize fabrication protocols.
Fabricated the embedded fiber-optic sensor using 2 fibers held a fixed distance apart with microcatheter tubing.
Designed the wrist-mounted housing and explored miniature custom fiber couplers for a future miniaturized revision.

sections.title: Mechanism
body: The sensing concept converts artery-driven deformation into a measurable optical signal.
bullets: Light is transmitted between two aligned optical fibers, across a gap maintained between the fibers by means of a short length of microcatheter tubing.
Arterial pulses deform the sensor face, and the fluid-filled PDMS pouch transmits that force to the fiber joint.
Fiber misalignment changes optical transmission, producing a continuous pulse waveform for downstream processing.

sections.title: Results
body: The final prototype demonstrated continuous wireless signal capture and preliminary blood-pressure prediction within the project target.
bullets: Data was collected from 14 participants under resting and post-exercise conditions.
The preliminary model achieved mean absolute errors of 3.38 ± 4.00 mmHg for systolic pressure and 2.87 ± 3.28 mmHg for diastolic pressure.
The sensing hardware reached wearable scale, while electronics miniaturization remained future work for a V2 revision.

projects.title: GPU-Accelerated Diffraction & Lens Simulator
projects.blurb: Interactive wave-optics simulation tool for modeling optical propagation and lens behavior.

sections.title: Overview
body: Built a Python-based optical simulation tool for modeling scalar diffraction, lens focusing, and image-quality metrics in configurable optical systems.
bullets: Developed the project to make diffraction simulations faster, more interactive, and easy to use.
Focused on realistic propagation through lens systems rather than simple textbook ray diagrams.
Used the simulator to explore how geometry, wavelength, aperture size, and lens configuration affect optical field propagation and focusing behavior.

sections.title: Simulation Method
bullets: Implemented scalar wave-optics propagation to simulate 2D XZ-plane optical intensity fields through lens systems.
Represented optical components as refractive-index structures on a simulation grid, allowing arbitrary lens geometries to be placed in the optical path.
Supported multi-element lens systems, configurable wavelength, field angle, refractive index, aperture size, grid resolution, and propagation distance.
Propagated optical fields using a Fourier-domain split-step wave propagation method, alternating between propagation in spatial-frequency space and refractive-index updates in real space.
Generated intensity maps that show beam propagation, focusing, diffraction effects, and field evolution through the simulated optical system.

sections.title: GPU Acceleration
bullets: Implemented the numerical simulation backend in PyTorch to support GPU acceleration for large grid-based optical calculations.
Achieved approximately 10x speedup compared with CPU execution on open-source libraries like DiffrctIO, making parameter sweeps and design iteration more practical.
Used vectorized tensor operations to reduce simulation time and keep the tool responsive during interactive design changes.

sections.title: Optical Analysis
bullets: Added analysis tools for point spread function, modulation transfer function, effective focal length, and back focal length.
Used simulated intensity fields to compare focal spot size, focal position, and image-quality behavior across different lens parameters.
Created visual outputs for lens geometry, refractive-index distribution, propagated intensity, and performance metrics.

sections.title: Interface & Workflow
bullets: Built a Streamlit interface for adjusting simulation parameters, running models, and visualizing results without editing code.
Designed the UI around fast iteration, with controls for source parameters, grid settings, optical components, and analysis outputs.
Used plots and image-based visualizations to make optical behavior easier to interpret and debug.

projects.title: Semiconductor Device Fabrication Labs
projects.blurb: Cleanroom fabrication and characterization of MIS capacitors and surface-micromachined MEMS actuators.

sections.title: Overview
body: Selected university cleanroom labs focused on semiconductor device processing, thin-film deposition, photolithography, etching, and device characterization.
bullets: Fabricated and characterized MIS capacitor and MEMS actuator devices using multi-step cleanroom process flows.
Connected fabrication steps, film properties, device geometry, and electrical measurements to final device behavior.
Built practical experience with semiconductor processing, process documentation, metrology, and device-level analysis.

sections.title: MIS Capacitors
bullets: Fabricated metal-insulator-semiconductor capacitors using photolithography, PECVD SiN deposition, sputtered Al metallization, RIE, and wet etching.
Characterized film thickness, pattern transfer, and device structure using ellipsometry and Dektak stylus profilometry.
Measured device behavior using I-V and C-V characterization to evaluate leakage and capacitance response.
Analyzed measurement results to connect dielectric quality, interface behavior, and fabrication variation with observed device characteristics.

sections.title: MEMS Actuators
bullets: Fabricated surface-micromachined MEMS actuator structures using photolithography, PECVD SiN deposition, DC sputtering, wet etching, and RIE release.
Used thin-film patterning and release-style processing to create suspended MEMS structures from deposited device layers.
Characterized fabricated devices using four-point probe measurements, stylus profilometry, optical microscopy, and I-V/C-V measurements.
Evaluated how film properties, process tolerances, etch behavior, and release quality affected final MEMS actuator geometry and performance.

sections.title: Characterization & Analysis
bullets: Used ellipsometry and profilometry to verify film thicknesses, step heights, and process outcomes after deposition and etching steps.
Used optical microscopy to inspect lithography quality, pattern fidelity, alignment, and post-release device structures.
Performed electrical characterization to compare fabricated device behavior against expected semiconductor and MEMS device response.
Documented process results and interpreted fabrication issues through measured electrical, optical, and geometric data.

projects.title: Autonomous EV Charging Location Optimizer
projects.blurb: Mixed Integer Programming model to optimize locations for autonomous EV charging stations.
bullets: Built a Python geospatial pipeline using OSMnx/NetworkX to pull the city road graph, generate candidate station sites, and compute network-based travel distances.

Formulated a Mixed-Integer Programming facility-location model to place new L2/DC fast-charging sites and optionally acquire/retrofit existing stations (from OpenChargeMap) under budget and capacity constraints.
Modeled demand as weighted nodes (weighted by the city's point-of-interest density) and minimized the demand-weighted travel distance for charging from each demand node using GurobiPy.

Implemented constraint logic for real-world feasibility (site selection, station capacities, upgrade decisions, and budget tradeoffs) and ran scenario sweeps to study how solutions change with assumptions.
Generated map-based visualizations of demand density and station locations to make the output interpretable and easy to validate.

projects.title: Shop-Built 2x72 Belt Grinder & Surface Grinding Attachment
projects.blurb: Designed and fabricated a 3 hp 2x72 belt grinder and precision surface-grinding attachment for bladesmithing and metal fabrication.
bullets: Designed and built a 3 hp variable-speed 2x72 belt grinder for knife making, metal fabrication, and precision grinding workflows.
Built the grinder around standard 1.5" tooling arms to support modular attachments, contact wheels, platens, small-wheel holders, and work rests.
Designed a tilting frame and belt-tracking system to support horizontal and vertical grinding configurations.
Fabricated the grinder using CAD, CNC laser-cut parts, welding, manual machining, fitting, and assembly.
Designed and machined a surface-grinding attachment with a rigid dovetail feed mechanism and UHMW gibs for smooth, controlled travel.
Built a switchable-magnet chuck with an integrated sine-bar feature to hold workpieces securely and grind controlled tapers.
Used the project to develop practical experience in machine design, fabrication tolerance stackups, rigidity, alignment, and iterative mechanical debugging.
